item.title: Too $hort Explains Why He Passed On A Trump-Linked Appearance
item.dc:creator: Mike Winslow
item.description: Too $hort draws a line between voter registration shows and a political invitation he felt would signal support for Trump.
item.content:encoded:
Too $hort turned down a political appearance because he thought getting onstage would look like an endorsement of Donald Trump.

The Oakland rapper said in an interview on Flagrant and Funny that the invitation came from a Trump supporter, not directly from someone in the president’s circle.

Too $hort told hosts Cari Champion and Jemele Hill that he saw the event as political even without a phone call from Trump’s team.

“I don’t want to align myself with that because it’s just something that I wasn’t supporting,” Too $hort said. He didn’t name the person who approached him or identify the event.

That’s different from how Too $hort described the voter registration concerts he has done through Democratic organizers.

He said the shows were free to the public, with registration part of getting in, but nobody was told whom to vote for.

He remembered being offered twice his usual fee for a Milwaukee appearance and drew a line between getting people to register and letting an appearance stand as support for a candidate.

Too $hort didn’t describe the Trump-linked invitation as a million-dollar offer, either.

The interview turned to whether someone might reconsider if offered $1 million for two appearances, and he said he hadn’t faced that choice.

Too $hort has pushed back before when his name was used to suggest he backed Trump.

In 2020, he publicly rejected how a documentary grouped him with Trump supporters and said at the time that he had passed on a separate effort to get him to travel to Washington to meet with the president.

In the new interview, he focused on how somebody can read a political message into an artist simply taking the stage.

The conversation about political invitations followed a question about former Vice President Kamala Harris. Too $hort said the two move in some of the same circles but pushed back on the suggestion that they’d previously bumped into each other.

Asked about Kamala Harris being a Too $hort listener, the rapper joked that he would’ve pegged her as more of an MC Hammer fan.

item.title: Ja Rule Considers Giving His Album An AI-Generated 70s Makeover
item.dc:creator: Nolan Strong
item.description: Ja Rule hears a familiar hit recast in a different era and weighs bringing that sound to an entire album from his catalog.
item.content:encoded:
Ja Rule heard artificial intelligence turn “Put It On Me” into a record that sounded like it came out in the 1970s, and now he’s considering giving a whole album the same treatment.

“I’m thinking about repurposing like one of my whole albums like that and just put it out as a ’70s vibe,” Ja Rule said in a Yahoo Finance interview.

He described the reworked single in four words: “It sounded fucking amazing.”

The song that caught his attention is from Rule 3:36, his second album, released in 2000.

The original album recording features Vita, and the version credited on Billboard’s Hot 100 with Lil’ Mo and Vita reached No. 8 in March 2001. Tru Stylze and Irv Gotti are credited as producers on the album recording.

The original song earned Ja Rule and Vita a Grammy nomination for Best Rap Performance by a Duo or Group.

Ja Rule also said he’d consider using the technology before a song is recorded, not just after it’s out.

When he writes for other singers, he said he has used a vocalist to record a guide so they can hear how the song is meant to go. He said a generated voice could do that job instead, or potentially stay on a song he wrote if he liked the result.

“Now I don’t have to do that if I don’t want. I could write this record, you know, feed it to the AI model, let it sing it and then send it to the artist. Or actually say, wow, this sounds amazing with the AI voice. Maybe I’ll leave it and put it out as an AI song,” Ja Rule said.

Ja Rule’s interest in making another version of an older album comes after he’d discussed a possible sale of his catalog in 2023.

At the time, he said he’d want a deal that let his family buy back a share later. In talking to Sozzi about the music now, Ja Rule described streaming as a source of checks he wasn’t getting a decade ago.

Ja Rule told Sozzi that nobody had approached him to make AI music when the host asked whether he’d been pitched a project.

item.title: Jay-Z Reveals Muhammad Ali Wanted To Punch Him In The Face
item.dc:creator: Mike Winslow
item.description: Jay-Z laughs about his run-ins with Muhammad Ali and explains what sold him on the actor playing his childhood hero.
item.content:encoded:
Jay-Z still laughs about the way Muhammad Ali welcomed him whenever their paths crossed.

The rapper laughed about it in Roc Nation’s roundtable for “The Greatest,” the Prime Video drama about Ali that Jay-Z helped bring to the screen.

The story came up when moderator Frazier Tharpe asked whether Jay-Z got to spend time with Ali.

“Yeah, for some reason he always wanted to punch me in the face,” Jay-Z joked, recalling how much he enjoyed the way Ali greeted him by putting a hand on his chin.

Long before those meetings, the boxer was a fixture on the television in Jay-Z’s childhood home in Brooklyn’s Marcy Houses.

“Ali was my first hero,” Jay-Z said as he described growing up in a household where music and sports were always on.

He said Ali taught him that having a public platform means accepting that people will disagree with you, telling Tharpe to “just do what you believe is right”; he also pointed to Ali’s example for younger people, saying fearlessness went hand in hand with hard work.

When the series needed someone to play the athlete Jay-Z grew up watching, the rapper paid attention to how Jaalen Best moved.

Jay-Z said Best’s footwork won him over and credited creator Ben Watkins with holding out for the right actor. Best said he auditioned about eight times over nearly 18 months and trained for nine months to play the boxer.

Best’s preparation covered a version of Ali who was still becoming the figure Jay-Z knew from TV.

Lonnie Ali, the boxer’s widow and one of the series’ executive producers, said the story follows him from his Olympic gold medal in Rome to his fight with Sonny Liston, including his family and upbringing in the segregated South.

Ali’s life outside the ring also shaped the series’ sound, which features a theme song from Wyclef Jean. The Fugees co-founder told AllHipHop he wanted to write a proper theme, and he made “Gladiator” with Watkins and singer Kofi Black.

All eight episodes premiered November 4 on Prime Video, where Michael Ealy plays Malcolm X opposite Best’s young Ali.

item.title: EXCLUSIVE: Nicki Minaj Hires New Lawyer Who Eyes Counterclaims In $275K Jingle Ball Fight
item.dc:creator: Mike Winslow
item.description: Nicki Minaj's new attorney asks for more time and says her possible counterclaims could top the $275,149.62 demand.
item.content:encoded:
Nicki Minaj has a new lawyer who says her own potential claims could eclipse the roughly $275K that a production company wants from her and her company.

Peter A. Cross told a New York court in a statement that he had been hired that afternoon to represent the rapper and Pink Friday Productions LLC.

Cross said he had reviewed the court filings but was still waiting for the records behind his clients’ side of the dispute.

“But I have not yet received any documents from my clients relating to this matter,” Cross wrote. “Nor have I received any documents that her attorneys may have regarding this matter.”

Instead, Cross based his early assessment on two conversations with Nicki Minaj.

“Based on those conversations, it would appear that those counterclaims will substantially exceed the amount claimed by the plaintiff,” Cross wrote. “That is my good faith belief based on my conversations with Ms. Minaj to date.”

The potential counterclaims also figure in Cross’ account of why the previous lawyers wanted out.

“I have reason to believe based on my conversations with Ms. Minaj that her desire to bring those counterclaims was at least one of the reasons her prior counsel sought leave to withdraw from the representation,” he wrote.

The outgoing firm’s own account was broader when attorney Bruce W. Bieber asked to withdraw, citing disagreements over strategy and a breakdown in communication.

Bieber told the court those problems had made it “unreasonably difficult” to represent the defendants effectively.

The change comes as 24/7 Productions seeks a ruling without a trial over work it says it did for the 2023 Jingle Ball shows and New York events for Pink Friday 2.

Pink Friday Productions has disputed that it still owes the money, while Nicki Minaj has fought the claim that she’s personally liable.

Cross asked for a pause until January 29, 2027 to answer that motion and seek permission to file the counterclaims.

In the filing, Cross said the defendants “may seek to join additional parties as Counterclaim-Defendants.”

Cross also asked the court to move a preliminary conference then set for January 5 to a date after January 29.

item.title: Stove God Cooks Confirms Finished Solo Album With Westside Gunn Behind It
item.dc:creator: Nolan Strong
item.description: Stove God Cooks says Westside Gunn executive-produced his next solo album and explains how the Swizz Beatz record changed.
item.content:encoded:
Stove God Cooks says another solo album is already finished before his long-delayed Swizz Beatz album has even come out.

The Syracuse rapper named the next project Pray for Powder and told Bootleg Kev that Westside Gunn executive-produced it.

Gunn’s role doesn’t make it a joint album, something Stove God Cooks cleared up when Kev asked whether both rappers were on the billing.

“That one is already done,” Stove God Cooks said. He also said the project would go through Warner.

That would extend the Warner relationship beyond the release Warner and Babygrande Records had already announced, All This For Me? Stove God Cooks said Warner initially wanted to work with him rather than specifically pursuing the Swizz Beatz album.

The label’s interest shifted after he played the music in the meeting, he said.

Stove God Cooks also described a change to the version of All This For Me? that nearly came out earlier this year.

“There was a few joints that the sample just, we just couldn’t clear it,” he said, explaining that they swapped out those tracks.

He said the replacements improved the album rather than simply getting it out the door. Seeing Gunn record a project in a couple of days and get it out by Friday had sharpened his frustration with how long his own records took to release.

Swizz’s work remained at the center of the album after the changes, but Stove God Cooks said his role was production rather than a vocal feature.

The Swizz-produced “STOVIE’S HOME (Down Down)” restarted the rollout after the original March release date passed. The rapper named Jadakiss and Pusha T among the guests and said some Swizz ad-libs they recorded didn’t make the cut.

Stove God Cooks has kept releasing guest verses and hooks during the wait for a follow-up to the Roc Marciano-produced Reasonable Drought.

He said he sent Pusha back a first-pass hook for “F.I.C.O.” before realizing the song was headed for a Clipse album, and Pusha told him to leave the hook as it was.

Stove God Cooks said Gunn urged him to deliver his albums during their earlier conversations about his situation, before taking on the executive producer role for Pray for Powder.

item.title: 2Pac’s Said He Was Gonna F Mobb Deep In Angie Martinez’s Netflix Series
item.dc:creator: Houston Williams
item.description: 2Pac’s graphic challenge to the Queens pair finally reached viewers, bringing one of rap’s most bitter rivalries back into focus three decades later.
item.content:encoded:
2Pac threatened Mobb Deep in a 1996 interview at his Los Angeles home as his feud with the Queens rap duo intensified. Angie Martinez kept the exchange off the radio. Three decades later, she plays it in The Tupac Tapes with Angie Martinez, a four-part series that premiered Friday on Netflix. 

Shakur aimed the remarks at Havoc and Prodigy and urged Martinez to air them. “I’m fucking both of y’all in the a** and sending you back to Queens like b*tches, stripped naked.” When Martinez told him she couldn’t play that on the radio, Shakur offered what he called a clean version. He restated the threat using the word sex.

Martinez told GQ she still finds that part of the interview difficult to hear. She said she shared the material with Havoc before the series came out and sought perspective from Outlawz member Edi I Mean.

“Yeah, it’s hard to hear. I hate that part so much, but it’s what was happening at that moment,” she said.

The series puts the archival audio in front of people with ties to that period, including people who knew Shakur, alongside radio hosts and journalists who can speak to what was happening around the recording. 

The feud had already spilled onto records. Shakur took aim at Mobb Deep on “Hit ’Em Up” and mocked Prodigy’s sickle cell disease. The duo fired back with “Drop a Gem on ’Em.” Havoc told the Recording Academy that Mobb Deep deliberately pulled the single from radio after learning Shakur had been shot in Las Vegas. The song still appeared on Hell on Earth, which came out after Shakur’s death. Havoc said the two sides never had a chance to settle the feud. 

Martinez said she aired roughly 12 minutes of a conversation that ran a little over two hours. She told Netflix she cut the tape by hand with a razor blade and chose to air portions in which Shakur explained that his quarrel was with particular people.

She feared other remarks could inflame a conflict in which gunfire had already become a reality. After Shakur died, the prospect of listeners treating the interview as his final statement gave her another reason to keep much of it private.

There are two radio decisions at the center of this story. Martinez held back Shakur’s words in 1996, and Mobb Deep pulled its answer after he was shot.

Decades later, Martinez returned to the exchange and made sure Havoc could hear what had stayed off the air before the rest of the public heard it.

item.title: Meek Mill’s Drake Reunion Record “Going Bad” Goes Diamond
item.dc:creator: Mike Winslow
item.description: Meek Mill lands two RIAA awards with the Drake reunion single hitting Diamond and his Philadelphia anthem at six-times Platinum.
item.content:encoded:
Meek Mill earned Diamond certification for the Drake record he once said he couldn’t get a straight accounting for.

The Recording Industry Association of America certified “Going Bad” on November 26, the same day it moved his solo track “Dreams and Nightmares” to six-times Platinum.

“Going Bad” has reached 10 million units in the United States under the group’s rules for digital singles, which count sales and streams.

It earned Gold in February 2019 and hit five-times Platinum in May 2020. Both new awards list Maybach Music Group and Atlantic Records as the labels. Under those rules, 150 qualifying on-demand streams count the same as one permanent download.

Meek has publicly drawn a line between the kind of milestone a plaque records and what he personally takes home.

In a 2022 social media Q&A, he said he’d asked how much “Going Bad” brought in and was told $24 million. “I was like how much did I make?” Meek wrote, as AllHipHop reported at the time.

Meek also said he called Drake about the track three days before “Championships” came out and thought Drake had done it for free. He said the label gave him a plaque after he asked what the record had earned him.

The studio reunion followed a public reconciliation at Drake’s TD Garden show in Boston in September 2018, where he brought his former rival out to perform “Dreams and Nightmares.”

The two had spent years at odds after Meek accused Drake of using a ghostwriter, following their collaboration on Meek’s “R.I.C.O.”

Drake answered with diss records including “Charged Up” and “Back to Back,” and later appeared on “Going Bad” when Meek released Championships that November.

item.title: Snoop Dogg & Feid Take Their Inglewood Connection Into The Studio For Thanksgiving
item.dc:creator: Mike Winslow
item.description: Snoop Dogg and Feid turn a surprise Inglewood pairing into their first joint release with a Thanksgiving tribute to family.
item.content:encoded:
Snoop Dogg and Feid shared a Southern California festival stage before turning up together on a record for Thanksgiving.

The pair released “Gracias X Todo” on Thursday, after the Colombian artist previewed the song during a Latin Grammy performance that also brought DJ Premier into the mix.

The record marks their first release together after Feid brought Snoop out as a surprise guest at HARD Summer in Inglewood in 2025. That appearance gave Feid’s audience a run of Snoop’s own records, including “Drop It Like It’s Hot” and “The Next Episode,” before the two artists had a song of their own to play.

Their next public step came at the Latin Grammys in Las Vegas. Univision’s live coverage identified the preview in a set that included DJ Premier, Divino, Baby Ranks and Lil Supa.

Premier and Feid had already worked together on “Le Pido A Dios,” a Latin Grammy nominee for Best Rap/Hip-Hop Song.

Feid carried that stage preview into a video built around the people he wanted to thank. The clip uses photographs of his own family, pays tribute to his grandparents and ends in a candlelit church with the children’s choir from his GOOD KIDZ foundation.

Feid signs off with a dedication that credits the family members who helped make him who he is.

While Feid makes the family tribute personal, Snoop uses his verse to look back at starting out with little and being able to give back to people he loves.

Snoop has made room for Latin styles on his records before, including when he worked with Mexico’s Banda MS in 2020. That record, “Que Maldicion,” paired his rap with the band’s regional Mexican sound, whereas Feid brought him into the orbit of Colombian reggaeton.

Banda MS singer Oswaldo Silvas remembered the group’s surprise after seeing Snoop play their music following a Dodgers loss.

“We laughed thinking it was a meme,” Silvas told the Recording Academy.

Feid’s other connection to that Latin Grammy ceremony came through a record with another Colombian artist: He and Karol G won Best Reggaeton Performance for “Verano Rosa.”

item.title: Don Toliver Concert Probe Seeks More Than 100 Attendees After Manchester Evacuation
item.dc:creator: Mike Winslow
item.description: Police seek more than 100 people who were at Don Toliver's Manchester show as they investigate suspected organized robberies.
item.content:encoded:
Don Toliver‘s Manchester concert evacuation has police trying to reach more than 100 people who were at the show. Greater Manchester Police said Friday they suspect a “small group of organised criminals” singled out people in the Co-op Live crowd to rob. Detectives are in touch with authorities investigating similar incidents at two of Toliver’s other European shows.

“There are similar incidents at two Don Toliver gigs in Europe that are also relevant to our enquiries,” Assistant Chief Constable Tom Harding said. He didn’t name the cities or say the same suspects were involved. No one had been arrested as of Friday, and detectives were reviewing footage from security cameras and concertgoers’ phones.

That review follows the force’s earlier disclosure of nine reports of jewelry theft at the November 22 concert. On Tuesday, police said they were looking into whether the release of an unknown substance was connected to those reports and planned to speak to their counterparts in Europe. Detectives are still trying to identify the suspects and determine what they believe was released in Manchester.

That search began after arena staff called police shortly after 10 p.m. to report that people in the crowd were feeling the effects of an unknown substance. The force declared a major incident so police, medical crews and other agencies could respond together. More than 12,000 people were escorted from the building after the show was cut short.

The evacuation left 89 people showing symptoms police believed were linked to exposure, including eye and breathing irritation. Medics took one person to Manchester Royal Infirmary, while others received help at the scene before being moved to the nearby Etihad Stadium. Toliver’s two London shows were postponed until December, and ticket holders in Manchester were told they’d receive automatic refunds.

Harding said coverage of the evacuation could bring back memories of the 2017 bombing at a different Manchester arena. He drew a distinction between the two incidents, saying detectives aren’t dealing with the same kind of motive and acknowledging the distress the evacuation caused.

Harding also pointed people affected by the incident to the Greater Manchester Resilience Hub, which provides support after traumatic events.

item.title: Mood Brings Hi-Tek’s Cincinnati Vault To Vinyl
item.dc:creator: Nolan Strong
item.description: Mood turns a 2005 promo disc into a limited double LP with early Hi-Tek beats and sessions featuring Talib Kweli.
item.content:encoded:
Mood‘s 21-track collection of Hi-Tek productions is finally leaving the promo-CD bin. Space Invaderz is giving the Cincinnati crew’s self-titled 2005 compilation a two-LP pressing on Friday, November 27, with just 1,000 copies listed for participating independent shops.

The original CD was a promotional release, not a conventional album rollout, and the new edition pairs the original crew with the artists they met along the way.

The Record Store Day track list places the breakout single “Hustle On The Side,” featuring Vicious Lee, alongside a freestyle from Donte, Hi-Tek and Big D and “Illuminated Sunlight” with Sunz of Man.

Talib Kweli appears twice alongside Mood, on “Transmogrify” and “Industry Lies,” before turning up with Hi-Tek under their Reflection Eternal name on Donte’s “Human Element.”

Those credits capture the two before and after they teamed up: Hi-Tek recalled receiving Kweli’s demo after Mood came back from New York in a later conversation on Kweli’s People’s Party.

Mood had already put both Kweli and Hi-Tek on record by the time the group released Doom in 1997.

AllHipHop’s reporting on Main Flow traced the rapper’s beginnings back to his work with Donte and DJ Jahson and singled out “Karma,” which is also on these records.

“Mood and Tek set it off as far as getting paper for this music,” J. Sands of Lone Catalysts told AllHipHop while recalling the independent Cincinnati scene.

Kweli went on to make Train of Thought with Hi-Tek, but the producer told AllHipHop in an interview that his work with New York rappers didn’t define where he came from.

“I’m from Cincinnati, I ain’t from New York. I just happen to produce for a lot of New York rappers,” Hi-Tek said while explaining why he wanted his next album to make room for more of his hometown collaborators.

The compilation puts some of those Cincinnati connections on the same track instead of splitting them across solo releases.
